EVs have the largest consistent year-round impact (as shown by the average day impacts), increasing daytime loads over 5 GW on average and shedding approximately 1.5 GW of load in all hours of the evening. Space cooling adds an additional 5.8 GW at noon on the average day and sheds an average of another 2 GW in the late afternoon and early evening. On the peak net load day, the end use load response is noticeably different. Firstly, while EV load is reduced in the evening, it is not increased in the day. This is because EVs are considered to be flexible over a 3-day period, and on the peak day prices are consistently high enough to move all charging load into the neighboring days. Cooling daytime load increases are significant throughout the morning and early afternoon, adding 3-6 GW of load in all hours except for the 11am-12pm hour, when significant shed occurs. This enables a cooling load reduction of over 2 GW throughout the evening, with a cooling load reduction of 5.9 GW in the peak hour. Combined with all other end uses, the system net load is reduced 8.75 GW in the peak hour. Additional results presented in the report show the potential impacts of this highly coordinated load response, which could be an issue in the longer term, causing multiple daily ramping periods and new system peaks being set in previously low-price hours. Such new system load shapes could enable substantial increases in renewables integration, however, without requiring as much energy storage. vi Figure ES-3. Total system load impact on the average and peak day in response to the Full dynamic price design in the Low price scenario On a 2030 dynamic price profile, we find that the savings incurred by providing the modeled load response is significant. The total annual savings (per customer, for the given end use) is shown in Figure ES-4 for the Low price scenario. In the residential sector, the largest savings potential comes from Level 2 EVs, followed by Level 1 EVs and pool pumps. Commercial and Agricultural savings range widely across different sites due to the different scale of sites in each sector. Figure ES-4 shows up to the 90th percentile of savings; it should be noted that for Ag pumping, the 99th percentile is 3.1-3.6x the 90th percentile (depending on the utility and price design), while the 99th percentile of Commercial cooling and heating savings are 4-7x and 3-9x the 90th percentile, respectively. In all cases, bill savings significantly decline when moving from a Full, to Medium, to Mild tariff design. The flatter price shape of the Mild tariff offers less savings potential, which especially impacts the thermal loads that can only shift loads over relatively short time periods. Nonetheless, customers are saving hundreds of dollars on price response in most scenarios and end uses (space heating and all thermal loads on the Mild tariff being the primary exceptions). vii Figure ES-4.
